An (X) represents an optional or occasional user role in a mode. 14.3 Support Environment 14.3.1 Homeport It is envisioned that the MTV’s homeport will be at the FAU Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute (HBOI). Located in Ft. Pierce, Florida, HBOI is one of the nation’s premier oceanographic centers, with a research community of approximately 200 ocean scientists, staff, and students. The campus Final Technical Report 50/57 includes a 1000 m long and 40 m wide private channel with a turning notch and a small boat marina. The private channel is 7 miles from Ft. Pierce inlet via the Intracoastal Waterway with direct ocean access. This infrastructure was constructed and maintained to support the Johnson-Sea-Link I & II submersibles owned and operated by HBOI at FAU6. They were launched from HBOI’s previously owned research vessel R/V Seward Johnson7, a 204 ft, purpose-built, state-of-the-art vessel built in 1984 and redesigned in 1994, which displaces 1,282 tons and has a 6,000 nautical mile range. An experienced captain and crew maintained the R/V Seward Johnson as part of the University-National Oceanographic Laboratory System (UNOLS) fleet of research vessels. A team of highly skilled personnel operated, maintained, and upgraded the submersibles according to strict safety protocols. The Johnson-Sea-Link submersibles were built in 1971. The subs were in service for almost four decades, with 9,000 dives worldwide. Additional infrastructure includes a machine shop, fabrication shop, ample indoor climate-controlled warehouse space, pressure vessel test tank, clean assembly areas, dockside navigable waters access, onshore mobile cranes, power, fresh water, and several large tanks useful for pre-deployment ballast/buoyancy trimming. Figure 14-1: Overhead view of HBOI campus with private navigable channel. 14.3.2 Nearby Away Port In addition to direct port facilities available at FAU, several nearby ports offer dockage, marine services, fuel, and heavy lifting capabilities. Port of Ft. Pierce While the Port of Ft. Pierce is not one of Florida’s largest commercial ports, it does house one of mega yacht company Derecktor’s maintenance, repair, refit, and new construction facilities. It offers deepwater (26 ft. project depth) access with no overhead obstructions, eight acres of level concrete apron for storage and repair space, a refitted 40,000 sq. ft. building housing machine, wood, electrical, and pipe shops along with offices and other support services, and two bulkhead docks of 330 and 450 ft. lengths. The largest mobile hoist - 1,500 tons - in the U.S. and a planned 5,000-ton drydock provide unmatched flexibility and hauling capacity for mega yachts.
